comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C90-C95. Both recognize that experiments in snap29 RNAi cells validate that transport machinery is independent of fusion machinery. OpenEval provides detailed evaluation of the experimental design, while peer reviewers accept these confirmatory experiments without challenge.

Perfect agreement on claims C81-C88. Both accept the systematic Rab GTPase screen showing specificity of Rab7 and differential roles. OpenEval notes appropriate caution about Rab14 inference, while peer reviewers accept this as part of comprehensive characterization of Rab complexes.

Strong agreement on claims C3, C4, C39-C43, C46 regarding minus-end directed autophagosome movement. Both recognize high-quality microscopy and genetic evidence. OpenEval emphasizes converging evidence from multiple approaches, while peer reviewers acknowledge reliable Drosophila genetics and proper quantification.

Major disagreement on claims C32, C33, C35, C36. OpenEval finds validation controls well-supported, but Peer Reviewer 1 raises critical concerns that fusion-incompetence 'relies on citations from previous studies' and should be 'rigorously evaluated,' and critiques the logic in Figure 1-S1D as 'inappropriate.' This represents fundamental uncertainty about the experimental system.

Strong disagreement on claims C120-C123. OpenEval finds colocalization data supports that positioning affects fusion probability, appropriately distinguishing transport from direct fusion effects. However, Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly challenges this: 'this conclusion is not well supported... the possibility that the observed decrease is simply due to a direct defect in fusion, rather than an impairment of movement, has not been ruled out.'

Disagreement on claims C106-C110, C116-C119, C124. OpenEval finds strong support for volume-dependent fusion efficiency model from complementary loss- and gain-of-concentration experiments. Peer Reviewer 1 considers it 'a reasonable hypothesis' but raises major concerns that direct fusion defects haven't been ruled out, questioning the causal interpretation.

Disagreement on claims C107-C115 regarding autolysosome analysis. OpenEval finds the data supported, noting differential requirements. However, Peer Reviewer 1 raises critical methodological concern that 'both autophagosomes and autolysosomes are present' and 'it would be more appropriate to analyze autolysosomes and autophagosomes separately,' questioning whether structures can be reliably distinguished by size.

Agreement on claims C47-C51, C131-C132. Both accept the dynein/dynactin RNAi screen showing specific subunits are required. OpenEval emphasizes systematic screening and validation with dominant-negative constructs, while peer reviewers acknowledge the alternation of localization and well-controlled experiments.

Agreement on claims C57, C58, C60, C61, C137 regarding motor competition. Both accept kinesin overexpression causing peripheral accumulation and competitive motor relationships. OpenEval notes partial rescue indicating complexity, while peer reviewers state experiments 'largely support the authors' conclusions.'

Agreement on claims C63, C65, C67, C89, C153. Both accept Rab7-Epg5 and Rab39-ema interactions as important for autophagosome trafficking. OpenEval provides detailed evaluation of specificity and epistasis experiments, while peer reviewers summarize this as a strength moving the field forward.

Agreement on claims C72-C77, C80 regarding Epg5 as Rab7 effector. Both accept colocalization and biochemical interaction data. OpenEval emphasizes convergence of localization, biochemical, and functional data, while peer reviewers accept differential effects on autophagosomes versus lysosomes as part of characterization of distinct vesicle types.

Agreement on claims C96-C100, C103-C105 regarding parallel lysosome transport. Both accept shared requirements with specific exceptions. OpenEval notes differential effects of Epg5 and Rab2 provide mechanistic distinctions, while peer reviewers acknowledge the study extended findings by examining lysosomal movement.

Agreement on claims C1-C27 (background knowledge) and C28-C31, C125-C129 (methodological limitations). Both accept the literature review and identification of field limitations. OpenEval notes appropriate distinction between established facts and uncertainties, while Peer Reviewer 2 explicitly acknowledges the study 'moves the field forward by distinguishing between effects on pre- and post-fusion autophagosomes.'

Agreement on claims C78-C80. Both accept nephrocyte experiments showing Epg5 loss does not affect endolysosomal compartments. OpenEval emphasizes this as supporting Epg5's autophagy-specific function, while peer reviewers do not challenge these experiments.

Agreement on claims C37-C38. Both accept controls ruling out general organelle disorganization. OpenEval notes these are essential for interpreting positioning studies, while Peer Reviewer 2 acknowledges 'experiments are well controlled.'

Agreement on claims C53-C54. Both accept dominant-negative validation experiments for dynein requirement. OpenEval includes these as part of systematic validation, while peer reviewers do not challenge these supporting experiments.
Agreement on claim C62. Both accept kinesin localization to autophagosomes. OpenEval notes this supports the competition model, while peer reviewers do not challenge this mechanistic support.

Agreement on claims C55-C56. Both accept negative results with kinesin knockdowns. OpenEval emphasizes this strengthens the conclusion that dynein is the primary motor, while peer reviewers accept this as part of the overall motor competition model.

Agreement on claims C69-C71. Both accept epistasis experiments and differential effects. OpenEval notes Rab7 overexpression cannot rescue Epg5 loss supports the proposed pathway, while peer reviewers accept differential effects as part of Epg5 characterization.

Partial overlap on claim C102. Both address differential requirements for organelle types. OpenEval includes this in parallel lysosome transport analysis, while peer reviewers accept it as part of distinguishing pre- and post-fusion effects.

OpenEval finds claims C158-C159 (integrated model) well-supported by comprehensive experimental findings. No corresponding peer evaluation specifically addresses the overall integrated model, though peer reviewers generally accept individual components.

OpenEval finds claims C28-C30, C127-C129 (methodological limitations in the field) well-supported and representing valid critique. While peer reviewers acknowledge the study addresses pre- vs post-fusion distinction (R17), they don't specifically evaluate these methodological critique claims.

OpenEval finds claims C130-C133, C138, C142-C143 (conclusions about dynein subunits, kinesin regulation, reinterpretation of Rab14/Klp98A) well-supported. No corresponding peer evaluation specifically addresses these interpretive conclusions, though related experimental data are accepted.

OpenEval finds claims C31, C125-C126 (motivation and knowledge gaps) appropriately supported by citations. Peer reviewers acknowledge the study addresses these gaps (R17) but don't specifically evaluate these motivational claims.

OpenEval finds claims C34, C139-C157 (integration with literature, novel contributions, differential pre/post-fusion roles) supported, noting some aspects remain speculative. No corresponding peer evaluation specifically addresses these integrative claims, though peer reviewers accept the study moves the field forward (R5, R6, R7).
